newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac's old job promises return to haunt him.
newsitem.headline: Chirac's old job promises return to haunt him.

text.p: A two-year-old promise by President Jacques Chirac to put the jobless top of his list of priorities and get them back to work could turn out to be a big handicap for his centre-right government as it heads into a snap parliamentary election.

Chirac may consider it unfair, but many voters will use next month's ballot to protest against record unemployment and the austerity policies he has imposed to ensure France will qualify to join a single European currency.

"Above all, I will do everything in my power to restore France's social cohesion and renew the Republican pact with the French people. Employment will be my constant concern," Chirac said in his inaugural address to the nation on May 17, 1995.

At that point unemployment was 11.7 percent of the workforce. Now it is up to a record 12.8 percent with nearly 3.1 million jobless at the end of February. More than one in three of them have been out of work for more than a year and one in five is under 25 years old.
The long lines of jobless are a drain on public finances, but the real threat they pose to the government is political.

The government says cutting the public deficit, including trimming a civil service which employs nearly one in five French people, is essential irrespective of the need to meet the economic criteria to join the euro single currency.
It says it is cleaning up after years of runaway, unsustainable spending under Socialist rule.

The government is basically relying on economic growth to create jobs, hoping for an improvement in the unemployment figures around the end of this year. But that will be too late to help the fortunes of Chirac's majority in the two-round election on May 25 and June 1.
Chirac has taken the huge gamble of advancing the election by 10 months to try to win his centre-right team a renewed five-year mandate to push on with cutbacks which no one likes.

Although the main opposition Socialist party is also committed to the euro, its argues that the austerity policy has become dogmatic and obsessive, hurting purchasing power, consumer confidence and therefore growth and employment.

The Socialists are promising government-support to create 700,000 jobs and a generalised shorter 35-hour work week without loss of pay to create recruitment opportunities and at the same time prevent a fall in purchasing power.

They warn against too much privatisation in a country where people cherish well supported public services, as shown in the widespread public sympathy for a railway strike which crippled the country for several weeks in late 1995.

The government defends its record on job creation, pointing to a law it introduced a year ago which offers private sector firms relief from France's heavy social security contributions when they shorten the work week to protect jobs.

Despite criticism within the centre-right coalition itself, the "Robien law" was held up earlier this week as an example of government success after an audit estimated that 50,000 jobs had been saved since its adoption in June of last year.
Labour unrest is continuing, although on a far smaller scale than the rail and wider public sector strikes against social security reform which paralysed the country in late 1995.

The campaign signal from the government is that more growth and healthier finances will create jobs and allow the government to do more tax-cutting. It is already committed to cuts worth 75 billion francs ($13 billion) overall in 1997-2001. But spending will stay under the knife.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe confirmed on Thursday that the state budget would be capped for the second year in a row in 1998, meaning spending cuts in real terms. Government sources say this policy is likely to be renewed each year over the next five years.
Opinion polls carried out before Chirac called the election on Monday show what the government has to contend with.
A CSA poll carried out on April 7-8 and published on Friday showed that nearly two-thirds believed he had failed to honour his pledge on unemployment.
On his pledge to lower taxes, the "carrot" with which he is now trying again to renew voter confidence as a counterbalance to spending cuts, 55 percent believed he had failed.

With the euro at the heart of an increasingly polarised right-left campaign, Chirac's allies in government must also be worried by a poll on Thursday showing 69 percent favoured another referendum on joining the single currency.

The poll showed 71 percent of those surveyed felt the euro would fail to reduce social inequality, and, perhaps crucially, that 73 percent felt the euro would not help cut unemployment. ($ = 5.786 French Francs) REUTER 251349 GMT apr 97
